title: Trump's Magic Words: How 'Complete and Total Endorsement' Changes the Game
summary: Imagine you're running a race, and the most popular kid in school shouts your name and says you're the best—months before the race even starts. That's what's happening in the Republican Party right now. President Trump is giving his 'Complete and Total Endorsement' to candidates way earlier than he used to. An NPR analysis found that in 2018, Trump's average endorsement came just seven weeks before a primary election. This year? It's seven months before. That means his chosen candidates have almost a full year of extra support before the big November vote. Trump's endorsements often sound the same, with promises to 'Grow our Economy,' 'Cut Taxes,' and 'Protect our always under siege Second Amendment.' Most of the time, his pick wins. But not always. In Iowa, his candidate for governor lost by a tiny margin. In Georgia, his guy lost in a runoff. Still, Trump's early backing clears the field—other Republicans often drop out when they see his post on Truth Social. It's like a golden ticket that can make or break a campaign.
why_it_matters: This shows how a single popular person can have a huge effect on who gets to run for office, which might one day affect rules in your school or community.

background_read: In the United States, political parties hold primary elections to choose which candidate will run in the final election.
Donald Trump, a businessman and former president, is very famous and his support can help a candidate win.
Many voters look to Trump's endorsements to decide who to vote for.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Trump and the Republican candidates he endorses.
WHAT: Trump is giving 'Complete and Total Endorsement' many months before primary elections.
WHERE: This is happening across the United States, especially in states like Iowa and Georgia, and on the social media platform Truth Social.
WHY: Trump's endorsements often clear the field and give his chosen candidates a big advantage in winning.

perspectives.description: They believe his endorsements help great candidates win and keep the party united behind strong leaders.
They worry that one person having so much power to decide who runs is unfair and shuts out other good choices.
They point out that early endorsements change campaign strategies, forcing other candidates to decide whether to stay in the race or drop out.
